title: Benny Goodman's 1935 band and Fletcher Henderson's charts
summary: Asked about Goodman, Gil recalls the 1935 band as a fan, praising the Henderson arrangements and Goodman's early tone.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Yes, well we've talked about the problems here for a while, let's move to something else for a few minutes, here, and in the early '50s, I'm really quite fascinated by your work during the early '50s. And you certainly wrote for and arranged for a number of outstanding instrumental and vocal artists. And I'm just wondering if we might talk a little bit about some of your experiences present or otherwise with some of them.
Benny Goodman for instance, what did you do for him, do you remember?
I was mostly a fan of Denny Goodman's. Not Benny Goodman himself but the band

Well Benny Goodman fell into the mood of those at the time. It's very hard to describe to anybody now what Benny Goodman was like in 1935. At that time he had a lot of fire and a tone on the clarinet which he (tone they were trying to reach?). Later changed to a legitimate tone which he has now. And what he plays with his jazz band now don't sound like nothing because he doesn't have that tone, that he had. So he fit in well with it. It wasn't as though he was like something removed from Fletcher's arrangements. He fit into them. The glove fit him at that time. So the band was really very good in that sense. Rhythmically he had some problems. Like the sound of the drums and all that kind of ( ? ) he wasn't too crazy about. But the arrangements were really beautiful. And also there were a few nice players too, Lionel Hampton.
